en: The *Mahāpadma-vyūha-maṇḍala-sarvapāpa-vidhvaṃsana-dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heavens, Chao San Dafu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying in the country of Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park, beneath an Aśoka tree in Campā.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of twelve thousand and fifty bhikṣus,
as well as Maitreya Bodhisattva and other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
together with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
They respectfully surrounded him as he preached the Dharma,
which was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; its meaning was profound and far-reaching,
and his pure conduct was entirely complete.
At that time, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī,
there was a great king named Brahmadatta,
whose body and mind were purely virtuous and who felt compassion for all sentient beings.
He nurtured all sentient beings upon that great earth as if they were his own children.
Once, when the king went out of the city to tour the Buddhist temples,
he arrived at the gate of a vihāra and gazed back for a brief moment.
A gatekeeper informed the assembly of noble ones:
"The Great King Brahmāyus is now at the gate, intending to enter the monastery.
Thereupon, the assembly of noble ones immediately ordered the administrative monks to arrange flower garlands.
Upon hearing this, the administrative monk opened the door of the hall;
though he searched for the flower garland, it was nowhere to be found,
yet he saw it upon the crown of the Buddha’s head.
He immediately took it and went with the senior monk and the rest of the noble assembly to welcome the king;
he then presented the flower garland that he held to him.
The king immediately accepted it and placed it upon his head.
After a brief moment, he suddenly felt a headache.
The king thought to himself, "Why is this so?"
"I must have come to suffer this affliction because I went out during the summer heat.
Thereupon, the King immediately paid his respects and took leave of the holy assembly, returning to the palace and addressing his attendants: [text continues].
"I suffer from a headache and intend to bathe now;
you should quickly prepare scented water.
The king immediately removed all his ornaments and garments and proceeded to bathe.
There was a palace attendant who was skilled in attending to the king and washing his body.
After bathing for a long time, she suffered from a headache that would not subside.
The king then issued a decree summoning physicians.
The physician arrived, and the king then said to him:
"Because of the summer heat, I went out of the city to wander;
on the road, I became afflicted with a headache."
"Even though he was bathed in this way, his illness did not improve. What do you think?
The physician replied:
The King’s ailment was caused by internal heat;
he immediately applied ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*) to his body.
The King followed the advice and applied the sandalwood, yet his condition did not improve.
During the day and night, he experienced great suffering and distress.
Consequently, all the physicians went together to the king's presence,
looked at one another, and spoke these words:
The cause of this illness is unfathomable, and we harbor deep sorrow and distress.
"Since the King is thus, what skillful means can we employ to free him from his ailment?
While they were thus conversing, the King had a younger sister named Subhadrā.
Having resolved upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), he was filled with faith, reverence, and compassion.
Seeing the king’s suffering, his heart was struck with fear;
he stroked the king’s head with his hand and addressed him, saying:
"How is it that you are so terrified, like a coward? The king then replied,
"Subhūti, I do not know."
"How can one attain freedom from suffering and fear?
The sister spoke again, saying,
"If the King would thus request to go to the Buddha's dwelling..."
"The Buddha, endowed with great compassion, will surely provide salvation.
The king then said, "What you have intended is excellent, most excellent!
Because I forgot, I must go there this very moment."
He immediately commanded his high ministers to quickly arrange carriages, palanquins, and mounts.
At that time, the charioteers harnessed five hundred chariots;
the King, together with his retinue and all his officials, [prepared to depart].
Having departed from outside the city,
he went to the Jambū tree of no-sorrow and approached the place where the Buddha was.
On the way, there was a woman carrying firewood for her livelihood.
Carrying a bundle of firewood on her shoulder, she was producing it by the roadside.
When the King’s sister saw her, she could not bear to look;
covering her face with her hands, she fell to the ground in a faint.
When the king saw this, he immediately questioned his younger sister, saying, "What is it that afflicts you?
Tell me. The king's queen was named Surasundarī.
Reflecting thus in his mind, he addressed the king, saying:
"That Sūrpāraka lay fainting on the ground because he saw a woman carrying firewood by the roadside."
The suffering of giving birth to her son was exceedingly profound;
out of compassion, the sister could not bear to see it and thus acted accordingly.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately informed the queen.
The retribution for past karmic offenses cannot be evaded.
The King ordered palace attendants to bestow wealth and goods upon him to relieve his poverty, so that he might quickly return home.
His younger sister, fainting with distress, fanned him with a whisk to cool him;
she then regained consciousness and spoke again:
"Namo Buddhāya, Great King!"
"The poor woman suffers greatly; I cannot bear to see it.
Proceeding forward in succession, they saw a grove of trees in the distance.
Drawing closer to the monastery, the King then descended from his carriage.
Holding a vessel of ghee in his hand, he entered the grove and beheld the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, like a magnificent mountain of gold,
emitting a great radiance comparable to hundreds of thousands of suns.
Upon seeing this, the king immediately released his sister’s hand;
he bared his right shoulder, removed his crown,
and approached the Buddha with palms joined in reverence.
Having circumambulated the World-Honored One and prostrated at his feet, he remained prostrate on the ground for a long time.
Then the World-Honored One extended his golden arm, stroked the crown of his head, and said to the king: "Arise, arise!"
Upon hearing the Buddha’s command, the king rose immediately.
Within a mere kṣaṇa, his headache was completely cured.
His body and mind became refreshed and joyful, and the king was filled with great delight.
At that time, Subhūti was seated in one place together with his retinue.
Seeing that his sister’s countenance was sorrowful,
the king immediately asked her why she was so distressed, and she was made to question the Buddha.
Having heard this, the sister immediately rose from her seat, bared her right shoulder, and knelt with her right knee on the ground.
With palms joined in reverence, she gazed up at the Blessed One’s countenance and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One."
"Great King, last night you suffered greatly from a headache.
Your royal kinsmen and ministers were all filled with anxiety and distress;
because of this matter, they have all come together to the place where the Buddha is."
Along the way, he saw a woman carrying a load of firewood;
she was dressed in tattered clothes, her hair was disheveled,
and she was crying out as she gave birth to a child.
"Upon seeing this, we were struck with great terror and developed a profound revulsion for the female body.
World-Honored One, how may we escape this female form?
Furthermore, this Great King suffers from a headache."
Though eminent physicians had attempted to treat me, I could not be cured;
now, having received the World-Honored One’s hand upon the crown of my head,
I have attained peace and happiness in a mere instant.
"By what causes and conditions does this occur? We pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will explain it for us.
When the World-Honored One heard these words, he emitted a great radiance from his face.
Possessing various colors, they illuminated boundless and immeasurable worlds;
then these rays of light re-entered [the Buddha's] mouth.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda—
Seeing the Buddha’s radiance illuminating the world,
his heart was filled with doubt due to the Buddha’s majestic power;
he immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms, and paid respectful homage.
Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions does the Great Radiance issue forth today, universally illuminating the Buddha-fields?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly explain this for me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In a past age, within this city..."
There was a great king named Dīpāṅkara.
That king’s queen was named Aśokā,
and his second wife, whom the king cherished and esteemed, was named Anupamā.
On the borders of that kingdom was a small country whose ruler led his troops to invade the great kingdom.
At that time, King Dīpāṃkara immediately marshaled the fourfold army.
Accompanied by elephants, horses, chariots, and various ministers,
they performed music as they followed him out of the city to wage a punitive expedition.
On the way, the king halted his army for a brief moment.
At that time, Queen Anupamā realized she was pregnant and about to give birth;
she informed the palace women and ordered those inner officials.
He reported all that had occurred to King Jyotiṣprabha.
When the inner official had finished reporting this matter,
the king immediately issued a decree ordering the lady to return to the palace.
Since it was difficult for the lady to give birth after her return,
he immediately dispatched the minister Caṛika to report these matters in detail to the King with all haste.
Having heard this, the king immediately mounted his carriage and returned to the palace.
Upon arriving at the lady's quarters, he greeted her and offered words of comfort.
The king, seeing the suffering of his wife’s childbirth,
burned incense and poured out water before the Triple Gem, offering prayers and making a vow.
He gave the remaining water from that libation to the lady to drink.
At that time, Queen Aśokā, harboring feelings of jealousy,
took the king’s hand and said to him, "Lady Anupamā."
Their dispositions were deranged and they lacked all sense of shame;
naked and with disheveled hair, they were no different from gods or ghosts.
When the King heard this, he felt ashamed and turned away without looking back.
In a brief moment, Anupama was born as the crown prince; his body was of a true golden color,
his marks and signs were dignified and majestic, and his merit and virtue were perfectly complete.
He immediately presented the prince to the Great King.
Upon seeing him, the King’s heart was filled with great joy.
After a short while had passed, the palace women gathered together.
There was one person who said that Queen Aśokā was jealous;
when she heard these words, Lady Anupamā suddenly questioned her attendants and ordered them to explain the matter in detail immediately.
At that time, the palace attendants did not dare to conceal anything and recounted the previous events in detail.
Upon hearing these words, Queen Anupamā felt as if her heart were being torn apart, and she spoke, saying:
"What madness is this? What shamelessness!
he cried, beating his breast and collapsing to the ground in a state of delirium and distress.
At that moment, the palace attendants sprinkled water on his face and fanned him with whisks to cool him.
After a long time, he did not regain consciousness, and because of this, his life came to an end.
At that moment, the palace ladies wailed aloud;
the King, suddenly hearing their cries, was struck with extraordinary alarm and wonder.
The Emperor issued an edict ordering an inner official to go and inquire into the cause.
The inner official, having received his mandate, questioned the gatekeeper of the Palace of the Serpent (Shou-gong).
At that time, the gatekeeper of the Palace of the Serpent in turn questioned the palace women.
"O King, please understand quickly why we are weeping.
Then those palace attendants, their voices choked with grief and tears, immediately reported:
"The lady Anupamā has suddenly passed away."
"Therefore, the wailing and weeping should be reported to the King immediately.
At that time, having heard these words, the ministers were filled with sorrow and distress;
with faces bearing expressions of grief, they hurried before the King.
The King saw him from afar and, knowing that some calamity or affliction had occurred,
immediately asked the messenger, "Is it perhaps the Prince who is ill,
or the Queen? The messenger replied, "Now, Lady Anupamā has suddenly passed away."
Upon hearing this, the king was deeply stricken with grief and distress;
like a tree whose roots have been severed, he fainted and fell to the ground.
Then, the ministers sprinkled water upon his face, and after a long while, he regained consciousness.
The ministers submitted, saying: "Please, Your Majesty, set your mind at ease and do not give way to grief or distress.
There are hundreds of thousands of palace ladies and beautiful women who shall ensure the Great King’s constant increase in joy and pleasure."
Upon hearing these words of consolation, the king was immediately restored to health.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"She who was Queen Aśokā in a former life and gave rise to a heart of jealousy..."
The one who has now given birth by the roadside while carrying firewood for a poor woman is the former Anupamā, whose nature was compassionate;
the present Subhadrā is she.
Ānanda, what do you think?
If a person frequently practices greed and jealousy, they will,
in a future life, receive the great and undesirable retribution of evil fruits.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If King Brahmadatta suffers from a headache,
for the sake of the king, enter the grove."
The senior monk ordered an administrative monk to take the flower garland and go out to receive the king;
at that time, the administrative monk was named Viśākha.
The young people born later have distracted bodies and minds, and their natures and conduct are coarse and violent;
upon entering that hall, as there were no other flower garlands,
they [placed them] directly atop the Buddha’s head.
She immediately took the flower garland and offered it to the king.
Once the king had accepted it, he placed it upon his head;
after a mere moment, he suffered from a headache.
This caused all his ministers and retinue to fall into deep sorrow and distress.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words that cause and effect are never erroneous,
the king immediately confirmed them, saying, "So it is, so it is."
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Dṛḍhamati who rose from his seat amidst the great assembly,
bared his right shoulder, and joined his palms toward the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
if there are sentient beings who take money or goods belonging to a permanent endowment for their own personal use, what karmic retribution will they receive?"
The Buddha said, "When this person's life ends, they will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying, "How may this person be rescued? How may they be comforted? What shall serve as their guide?"
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right hand and addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: “Speak, speak!
You possess a mantra ritual manual of great compassion.”
It is capable of delivering all sentient beings.
If these sentient beings have entered the Avīci Hell,
this mantra is now well-able to rescue, comfort, and act as their sovereign.
When the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara heard these words,
he rose from his seat, joined his palms, and said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One, listen attentively."
"I possess the Great Compassion Heart Dhāraṇī,
which can bring vast benefit to all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!"
"I now listen attentively as it is sealed with the Great Vajra Seal.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara again addressed the World-Honored One.
This great vidyā-dhāraṇī of mine definitively eliminates all karmic offenses,
all evil destinies, and all suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, it causes sentient beings to dwell securely in the path to Bodhi.
This mantra is now subtle, wondrous, and most supreme;
like a great jewel tree, it is able to fulfill all aspirations.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, you should now simply proclaim the heart-mantra of the inconceivable, vast, and magnificent lotus-adorned maṇḍala."
May this mantra of invincible great power fulfill all the aspirations of sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
Having seen the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he made such a request for a second and third time;
then, bowing his head to the Buddha’s feet in prostration,
he stood before the Buddha and recited this Mahākaruṇā-citta-dhāraṇī.
Namo ratnatrayāya | Nama āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya ||
Nikāya-tan-yatha | paṭṇami paṭṇami paṭṇama-pratisthite | paṭṇo-nara-mahā-maṇḍala-mi-yuhi-sara-sara-kara ||
Kara kīri kīri kuru kuru mahābhaya samādhi duna duna viduna viduna hiriṃma mahāvinaye śodhaya śodhaya sarvajagadmapalaṃpa.
Rāṇimi buddhe buddhe mahārjuna-pratīccha svāhā. At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara...
Having spoken this Great Compassion Great Vidyā Dhāraṇī,
the entire great earth shook in six ways,
and all the celestial palaces and nāga palaces [trembled].
Furthermore, the palaces inhabited by all the yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas,
kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth, all shook violently.

All the Māra kings were seized with great terror and their hearts were filled with grief and distress; all the evil nāgas and various malevolent spirits fainted and fell to the ground, vanishing and becoming invisible.
All sentient beings in the hells,
receiving the light of the mantra, have the darkness of their karmic suffering shattered;
they immediately attain liberation and are reborn in the heavens.
With celestial *utpala* flowers, *kumuda* flowers, white lotuses,
*māndārava* flowers, and *mahāmāndārava* flowers,
they held them before that Buddha as an offering.
At that time, the World-Honored One,
emitting a vast and sublime Brahma-voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird,
praised the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
The dhāraṇī you have spoken is profound and inconceivable.
For the sake of all sentient beings,
you shall further explain the maṇḍala ritual procedures for the vast benefits of painting images and performing recitations.
Then the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, having received this instruction, spoke the ritual procedure:
"One must obtain a pure young girl who is suitable for the woolen thread and is observant of the precepts."
A person who has performed the purification ritual weaves it into a bolt of cloth,
four, three, two, or even one cubit in length;
it is then soaked in scented water and wound upon a spindle to be stretched out and purified through the ritual of binding.
For a person who upholds the precepts, one should paint an image on a scroll.
In the center of the scroll, first paint the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara seated upon a lotus throne,
with celestial garments draped across his shoulders and a crown upon his head.
Upon his crown is Amitābha Buddha,
adorned with all manner of ornaments;
his left hand holds a lotus flower.
His right hand forms the *varada-mudrā*.
To the left of Avalokiteśvara,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Śrī holding a white fly-whisk in his hand.
On the right side, paint the Bodhisattva Padmaśrī,
holding a lotus flower in his hand;
these two bodhisattvas each sit upon a lotus seat.
On the upper part of the cloth,
facing each other, paint two celestial beings holding flower garlands;
on the lower part of the cloth, [paint...]
Depict the Earth Goddess holding a lotus-flower parasol in her hand;
depict the two great nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda,
with their hands supporting the lotus seat of Avalokiteśvara.
To the right of that seat, depict the practitioner performing recitation,
kneeling with his right knee on the ground and holding a lotus flower in his hand.
In the empty spaces at the four sides of the painting:
Paint lotus flowers everywhere, endowed with various colors;
furthermore, on the lower part of the cloth,
paint the waters of the great ocean and the various classes of aquatic creatures.
Each of the *utpala*, *kumuda*, and white lotus flowers shall be fully blossomed.
Furthermore, one should use fine silk to paint a hundred-petaled lotus flower in four colors and place it before the cloth painting (*paṭa*).
Upon that lotus, present the five offerings.
Furthermore, one may also use rice flour, white flour,
or scented clay to fashion a wheel the size of a thumb.
Furthermore, every day offer eight hundred lotus flowers that have been moistened with white sandalwood water.
Also, use white sandalwood water to construct a maṇḍala.
Using the Lotus Mudrā, recite the aforementioned Lotus Mantra while offering flowers until one lakṣa have been presented.
This should be done on the eighth or fifteenth day of the bright fortnight.
Having observed the pure fast and precepts,
one should fashion eight hundred golden lotuses or silver lotuses,
creating eight kinds of vast and magnificent adornments.
Alternatively, one may make offerings with lotus canopies, lotus banners, and so forth. Furthermore,
within the painting, one should depict the assembly of holy beings in miniature and perform a grand offering using the five kinds of food and drink.
Having offered a single, exquisite, and wondrous lotus to the assembly of noble ones,
one should then perform the ritual for the consecration and celebration of the image.
All bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who possess faith [should participate].
By making offerings of vegetarian food and practicing such veneration,
all transgressions and sins committed previously— such as the misappropriation of the permanent property of Buddha images,
stupas, or monasteries— are entirely extinguished.
With their karmic obstructions purified, they shall not fall into the evil realms but will be reborn in a buddha-field.
At the time of death, while seated, they will behold the holy Avalokiteśvara within a pavilion of a maṇḍala adorned with vast lotuses.
He spoke words of consolation, saying, "Do not fear, do not fear!
You shall be reborn in a superior realm and shall no longer receive a female body.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, having spoken these words, [remained silent].
In that great assembly, there was a bodhisattva named Siṃhamati who rose from his seat,
joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
If King Brahmāyus, unaware that it was a flower garland upon the Buddha’s head, were to suddenly wear it,
he would experience a headache and great suffering within a mere kṣaṇa.

Furthermore, if there is a person who knows that these objects belonging to the Buddha’s images, stupas, and temples are intended for perpetual maintenance, yet takes them for their own personal use, what karmic retribution will they receive?
The Buddha said, "O Bodhisattva Siṃhamati: [listen]."
Excellent, excellent, that you are able to ask about this matter.
If King Brahmāyus has a pure mind and places his faith and respect in the Triple Gem,
even if he mistakenly wears a flower garland, [it will not be an offense].
As for those who obtain the present retribution of a headache:
it is like a single ink drop placed upon a clean white garment;
when the multitude sees it, the ink appears very small indeed.
If sentient beings in future ages should destroy or misappropriate the property of the eternally abiding Triple Gem,
it is like casting blue-black dye into an ink vessel;
the grave transgression incurred will be such that no other dharma can provide salvation.
Furthermore, Lion-Mind Bodhisattva,
if there is a faithful donor who relinquishes their wealth and profit to construct monasteries, stupas, and temples.
Whether it be images of merit or offerings made to the Triple Gem,
if a king or a high minister seizes the property from that monastic community for their own personal use;
This causes that bhikṣu to suffer poverty,
diminishes his majesty and power, and causes him to lose his vigor;
it cuts off his recitation and possession of mantras— such are the faults [of this].
Those kings and ministers shall incur great sin and suffering, no different from before.
If there is a bhikṣu who, despite possessing faith, understanding, eloquence, and wisdom,
delights in associating with kings and high-ranking ministers.
Seeking wealth and profit extensively, they become arrogant and conceited, violating the precepts.
I shall now further clarify this matter through a parable.
O Bodhisattva Siṃhamati, it is as if there were a person.
When one who is hungry consumes food and drink that contains poisonous medicine,
even if that medicine is but a single *liang*,
a single *fen*, or as small as a mustard seed.
Once that person has finished eating, they will certainly die;
it is the same for those who have left the household life:
relying on the power and influence of kings, they deceitfully seek wealth and profit.
"The offerings they receive are not sustenance for a right livelihood;
such a person will certainly incur an evil retribution.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhamati addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
If there are those who have left the household life and wear the dharma robes,
yet falsely seek wealth and profit with arrogance and conceit,
then even if kings, ministers, and others should honor and provide for them, they will derive no merit or benefit.
The Buddha said, "Siṃhamati Bodhisattva, do not speak thus.
It is like a person who has fainted and fallen to the ground;
by relying on another's support and assistance, he is immediately able to rise."
It is also like a great elephant sunk in the mud;
people are unable to lift the elephant's body out,
and it must rely on another elephant for support and assistance to emerge.
Furthermore, it is like a person who has received the consecration of a king,
yet at a later time loses that royal position;
ordinary people are then unable to protect him.
Only a powerful minister, possessing great majesty and valor, can restore the king to his throne.
O Bodhisattva Siṃhamati, it is likewise within my teaching:
whether there are those who rely upon the Dharma or those who do not rely upon the Dharma.
"All are children of the Buddha and shall all achieve benefit.
If one gives rise to contempt or disparagement, where could one obtain merit?
At that time, the entire great assembly, having heard these words, [was moved].
With one voice and in unison, they cried out in a loud voice:
"World-Honored One, we who have now been delivered by the Buddha have attained great joy and celebration.
May all sentient beings have their aspirations fulfilled."
The Buddha said: "If there is anyone who,
regarding this true dharma of the dhāraṇī,
either writes it themselves or causes another to write it..."
If one upholds, recites, and reverently makes offerings to it,
the merit obtained will be exceptionally superior and most sublime.
Furthermore, if there is another person who likewise...
Upon hearing the name of this second wheel of Dharma, the Great Power Dhāraṇī of the True Dharma transmitted by that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
such a person shall be considered one who has erected the banner of the Dharma, blown the conch shell of the Dharma, and deeply planted roots of goodness.
At that time, King Brahmāyus and the entire great assembly,
having conceived pure faith, rose from their seats,
joined their palms toward the Buddha, and made this vow:
May we henceforth never again encroach upon or appropriate the property held in perpetual endowment by the Sangha at Buddhist temples, stupas, and shrines— not even a single flower or a single fruit.
Furthermore, may four great monasteries be established at the four great city gates.
"May the Buddha bear witness that all these are adorned with the seven treasures.
The Buddha said: 'So be it, so be it! You should achieve this great benefit;
by remaining far removed from envy, you shall attain true tranquility.'"
At that time, King Brahmadatta, having made this vow,
circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to his own abode with his retinue;
he further preached this True Dharma for hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
He extensively practiced giving and constructed a great Buddhist temple.
At that time, the King’s sister, the laywoman Subhavyā,
was within the royal harem for the sake of five hundred thousand court ladies.
He extensively expounded the sublime Dharma and made a sincere vow.
Having made this vow, all the palace ladies transformed their female bodies and became men.
When all those people saw this, they were all greatly astonished and marveled;
they believed in and practiced the dharma of the dhāraṇī, and cried out in a loud voice: "Only the Buddha! Only the Dharma! Only the Saṃgha!"
The supreme field of merit is the true object of reliance.
If there are those who make offerings to or uphold this dhāraṇī,
such persons plant the roots of goodness for Buddhahood and shall obtain the highest merit.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra,
all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and those who are neither human nor non-human,
were filled with great joy; they received it with faith and departed.
The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī for the Extinction of All Sins through the Vast Lotus-Adorned Maṇḍala.
